examples.explain: Strings may contain '#' and may be empty - the encoding must still be unambiguous.

hints: Any single separator can appear *inside* a string. What extra information would make the boundaries unambiguous?
Either escape the separator, or tell the decoder up front how long each string is.
Length prefix: write len(s) + '#' + s. The decoder reads digits up to '#', then copies exactly that many characters.

insight.mnemonic: Say how long, then say it.
insight.oneLiner: Prefix every string with its length and a delimiter; the decoder jumps over the payload instead of scanning it.

recall.a: A string containing ',' splits into extra pieces when decoding.
recall.q: Why does a plain separator like ',' fail?

recall.a: Length-prefixed frames (or escaping), exactly as here.
recall.q: How do network protocols solve the same problem?

insight.why: The delimiter only needs to be unambiguous inside the header, which is digits - the payload is never interpreted.

oneLiner: Prefix every string with its length and a delimiter; the decoder jumps over the payload instead of scanning it.

pitfalls.explain: Splitting on a separator breaks as soon as a string contains it. Encode lengths, or escape.
pitfalls.title: A string contained your delimiter

pitfalls.explain: ''.split(',') returns [''], not []. Make sure [] and [''] round-trip differently.
pitfalls.title: Lost empty strings or the empty list

solutions.idea: Terminate each string with ';' and escape any ';' or backslash inside it, so the decoder can tell them apart.
solutions.name: Escape the delimiter

footnotes.text: The length tells the decoder exactly how far to read, so the string may contain '#', digits, anything - nothing is ever ambiguous.

solutions.idea: Write each string as <length>#<string>. Decoding reads the length, then slices exactly that many characters.
solutions.name: Length prefix

statement:
Design a pair of functions that pack a **list of strings into one string** and unpack it again.

- `encode(strs)` returns a single string.
- `decode(s)` receives that string and must return the original list exactly.

Strings can contain **any** printable character, including whatever separator you'd like to use - and they may be empty. The judge checks `decode(encode(strs)) == strs`.
title: Encode and Decode Strings
